body.text: Tasmania's cave explorers are still making discoveries after 80 years
Underneath Tasmania lies kilometres of sprawling networks of underground caves, including the deepest in the country.
The Southern Tasmanian Caverneers, the oldest caving club in Australia, has spent 80 years exploring this hidden world.
The club's vice-president Janine McKinnon has been caving for more than 50 years and, now in her 70s, is still venturing underground.

Over that time, she has seen technological innovations and cultural shifts that have transformed caving, allowing explorers to probe deeper than ever before into Tasmania's labyrinthine underground networks.
"What people can do with caving now and the skills they develop and the places they go just blows the past out of the water,"
She grew up in suburban Melbourne, a far cry from the subterranean worlds she would later be drawn to as a young woman.
While living in Canberra in the 1970s, she fell in with a caving community and became acquainted with the scientific study of caves, known as speleology.
It opened a world of possibilities: exploration, surveying, map-making, photography, the physical challenge of descending into the unknown, and the thrill of being at the vanguard of exploration.
"It's this sense of going into somewhere that is just so alien," Ms McKinnon said.
"You go into this void of just rock and maybe water, and it just is really telling you: 'I don't care if you're here or not.'"
Her passion for caving pulled her to Tasmania in the 1980s — home to "the best caves in Australia", according to Ms McKinnon — and eventually to the Southern Tasmanian Caverneers.
Eight decades of change

The Tasmanian Caverneering Club was founded in 1946 by Samuel Warren Carey, a geology professor at the University of Tasmania who had served in the Z Special Unit — a secret reconnaissance team operating behind Japanese lines in the south-west Pacific during World War II.
In 1996, it merged with two other caving clubs to form the Southern Tasmanian Caverneers.
Compared with today, caving gear in the early and mid-20th century was heavy and rudimentary.
Short vertical drops were navigated down using flexible metal wire "rope" ladders.
Deeper depths required a person to be belayed with a hemp rope, meaning someone was required to remain stationed at the top.
Ms McKinnon likened those early days to mountaineering expeditions: 20 people may walk to the cave entrance with huge amounts of gear, which was gradually deposited at each drop.
"We would just keep leaving people at the top of each drop with a rope and they would sit there for however many hours," Ms McKinnon said.

Now, with what's known as single rope technique to travel up and down vertical drops or "pitches", what may have taken an expedition of dozens of people to get to the bottom of a particular cave can now be done by three or four.

Improvements in specialised underground radio technology has made it easier to communicate, long-lasting LED head-torches have replaced the carbide mining lamps, and electronic survey devices are now used to help teams build accurate maps of caves.
Rescue training scenarios using complex, modern rope systems means teams are better prepared in case of emergencies.
And, crucially, their clothing has improved too.
In the last few decades, semi-waterproof suits, rubber-soled boots and lighter thermal gear have replaced the heavy woollen thermals and hobnail boots of yesteryear.
Pushing the frontier
Caving also opened a world of internal possibility for Ms McKinnon.
"Caving started a journey where the more I did, the more I appreciated how it helped you develop so many aspects of yourself that you didn't know were there," she said.
"You discovered where your fear levels were and where the things you couldn't cope with were."
But with that came a culture that could be male-dominated and unaccommodating for the few women in the scene.
More often than not, Ms McKinnon was the only female in the group, but in the past 15 years she said that culture had changed.
"It's become a lot more supportive, a lot more collegiate, a lot less just competitive," she said.
"I'm certainly much happier caving now than I was."
Ciara Smart, the club's secretary, is one of the next generation of cavers pushing the frontier of Tasmanian underground exploration.
"We've got a lot of really strong female leaders in the club, which perhaps wasn't always the case," Dr Smart said.
"I think it's a testament to the supportive nature of the club now that we've got fairly even numbers of men and women."
A common misconception, Dr Smart said, was that the great days of cave exploration in Tasmania were over.

In reality, the known network of Tasmania's caves — concentrated predominantly at Mole Creek in the state's north; the Junee Florentine karst region in the south-west; and Ida Bay in the south — is still growing.
"We don't have the luxury any more of entrances that you can discover easily, but we've still found huge numbers of caves in the last few years," Dr Smart said.

The deepest known cave in Australia, named Delta Variant, was discovered in the Niggly Cave system near Maydena, after several kilometres of new passages were found following breakthroughs in the last four years.
And this year, the 800th cave entrance in the Junee Florentine karst region was found, and is yet to be fully explored.
It was aptly named Octogenarian Anniversary.
A new generation
Fourteen-year-old Ben Jackson is among the youngest Tasmanian cavers and has grown up in the community.
Initially prompted to join the club by his father, who is an avid caver himself, Ben is unperturbed by the challenges and risks associated with caving.
"It's been pretty normal; it's just a thing that happens," he said.
Due to his thin frame, Ben often takes on the role of a "forward probe" to navigate narrow passages.
There are few pastimes that give people the opportunity to say they were the first human to set foot in an unexplored part of the world.
It's that feeling, and the camaraderie that comes with it, that pushes Ben and Dr Smart forward.
"Perhaps it's a 200-metre abseil, perhaps it's a gorgeous wall of glittering stalagmites,"
Dr Smart said.
"You just don't know. And that feeling is thrilling and it's fairly addictive."
